positions/two-sacraments/oneLine: Only baptism and the Lord’s Supper were instituted by Christ as sacraments of the gospel; for many evangelicals they are "ordinances" of obedience rather than means of grace.
positions/two-sacraments/coreClaims/0: A sacrament requires Christ’s explicit command, a visible sign and a promise of grace attached to it.
positions/two-sacraments/coreClaims/1: Only baptism (Matt 28:19) and the Supper (1 Cor 11:23–26) meet these criteria.
positions/two-sacraments/coreClaims/2: Confirmation, penance, orders, marriage and anointing are worthy rites or callings but not sacraments of the gospel.
positions/two-sacraments/coreClaims/3: For Lutherans, Anglicans and Reformed the two are means of grace; for Baptists and many evangelicals they are ordinances: acts of obedience that symbolise and proclaim grace received by faith.
positions/two-sacraments/origin: Luther’s The Babylonian Captivity of the Church (1520) reduced seven sacraments to three (baptism, bread, penance) and then effectively to two. The Augsburg Confession (1530), Zwingli, Calvin (Institutes 4.19), the Anglican Thirty-Nine Articles (XXV) and the Westminster Confession (27.4) all teach two. Anabaptists and Baptists (London Confession, 1644) prefer "ordinances".
positions/two-sacraments/strongestArgume: It ties sacramental status strictly to Christ’s explicit word, guarding against human additions.
Paul pairs the two rites as the Church’s defining signs (1 Cor 10:1–4; 12:13).
It refocuses worship on Word and faith rather than a priestly system.
positions/two-sacraments/strongestObject: Catholics and Orthodox reply that Scripture also attaches grace to the laying on of hands (2 Tim 1:6), anointing (James 5:14–15) and forgiveness by the apostles (John 20:23).
The number two is itself a 16th-century systematisation that the early Church did not know.
Within Protestantism, the "ordinance" view is criticised by Lutherans and Reformed as reducing sacraments to human acts (Zwinglianism).
positions/two-sacraments/responses/0: Protestants reply that other rites may be biblical and beneficial without being sacraments in the strict sense; Anglicans call them "commonly called sacraments".
positions/two-sacraments/responses/1: Baptists reply that ordinances honour Christ’s commands while guarding against belief that grace is conferred automatically.
positions/two-sacraments/consequences/0: Simplified Protestant worship and church life; ended clerical sacramental confession in most Protestant churches.
positions/two-sacraments/consequences/1: Marriage became a civil and religious covenant rather than a sacrament, eventually opening the way to legal divorce in Protestant lands.
positions/two-sacraments/consequences/2: Created intra-Protestant diversity between sacramental and ordinance views.
positions/transubstantiation/oneLine: At the consecration the whole substance of the bread and wine is changed into the substance of Christ’s body and blood, while the appearances (accidents) of bread and wine remain.
positions/transubstantiation/coreClaims/: Christ is truly, really and substantially present, body, blood, soul and divinity, under the appearances of bread and wine.
The change occurs through the words of consecration spoken by a validly ordained priest.
Only the appearances (taste, colour, extension) of bread and wine remain; their substance does not.
Christ remains present as long as the species endure, so the reserved sacrament is adored.
The Mass makes present the one sacrifice of Calvary.
positions/transubstantiation/keyTexts/4: Council of Trent, Session 13 (1551), ch. 4 and canon 2
positions/transubstantiation/origin: Patristic realism (Ignatius, Justin, Cyril of Jerusalem, Ambrose’s De Mysteriis) and the 9th-century Corbie debate prepared the way; after Berengar of Tours questioned a substantial change, Rome required him to confess it (1059, 1079). The term "transubstantiation" appears in the 12th century and in Lateran IV (1215); Thomas Aquinas gave it Aristotelian precision (Summa Theologiae III q.75–77); Trent (1551) declared it "fittingly and properly" named; Paul VI’s Mysterium Fidei (1965) reaffirmed it.
positions/transubstantiation/strongestAr: It takes Jesus’ words "this is my body" and John 6 ("my flesh is meat indeed") in their most direct sense.
The early Fathers consistently speak of the Eucharist as Christ’s flesh and of a change in the elements.
Paul warns that unworthy reception is guilt against "the body and blood of the Lord" (1 Cor 11:27), implying more than a symbol.
"Substance" is a metaphysical, not physical, claim, so it is not refuted by chemistry and protects both real presence and the reality of the appearances.
positions/transubstantiation/strongestOb: Protestants argue it depends on Aristotelian categories alien to Scripture and was unknown as such for a thousand years.
Reformed critics argue Christ’s human body is now in heaven (Acts 3:21) and cannot be locally present on many altars.
Jesus’ words in John 6:63 ("the flesh profiteth nothing ... the words that I speak ... are spirit") point to a spiritual reading.
Eucharistic adoration and the sacrifice of the Mass seemed to Reformers to detract from Christ’s once-for-all sacrifice (Heb 10:10–14).
positions/transubstantiation/responses/0: Catholics reply that the doctrine predates Aristotle’s rediscovery (Lateran IV, 1215) and that the term protects a mystery rather than explaining it.
positions/transubstantiation/responses/1: Christ’s glorified body is present sacramentally, not locally or by spatial multiplication (Aquinas, ST III q.76 a.5).
positions/transubstantiation/responses/2: The Mass is not a new sacrifice but the sacramental re-presentation of the one sacrifice (Trent Session 22; CCC 1366–1367).
positions/transubstantiation/consequence: Shaped medieval devotion: elevation of the host, Corpus Christi (1264), monstrances and processions.
A central issue in the Reformation and in the martyrdoms of Protestants (e.g. in Marian England) and Catholics.
Remains a key point in Catholic–Protestant dialogue, softened by ecumenical statements (e.g. ARCIC Windsor Statement, 1971).
positions/orthodox-eucharistic-mystery/o: Through the invocation of the Holy Spirit the bread and wine truly become the body and blood of Christ, a mystery to be received in faith rather than explained philosophically.
positions/orthodox-eucharistic-mystery/c: The gifts are truly changed (metaballo) into Christ’s body and blood.
The change is the work of the Holy Spirit invoked in the epiclesis of the anaphora, not of the words of institution alone.
The manner of the change is a mystery beyond definition; philosophical terms are secondary.
The Eucharist is the Church’s participation in the heavenly liturgy and the foretaste of the Kingdom, received by all the baptised including infants.
positions/orthodox-eucharistic-mystery/k: Liturgies of St John Chrysostom and St Basil (epiclesis)
positions/orthodox-eucharistic-mystery/o: Rooted in Greek and Syriac patristic teaching (Cyril of Jerusalem, Gregory of Nyssa, John Chrysostom, John of Damascus) and the Eastern anaphoras. Against Protestant influence (the Calvinist-leaning Confession of Cyril Lucaris, 1629), the Synod of Jerusalem (1672) under Dositheus used the term metousiōsis; many modern Orthodox theologians prefer to avoid scholastic categories. Oriental Orthodox and the Church of the East hold comparable realist views; Rome recognised the validity of the East Syriac Anaphora of Addai and Mari, which has no explicit institution narrative, in 2001.
positions/orthodox-eucharistic-mystery/s: It preserves the patristic language of real change without binding faith to a medieval philosophical system.
It gives the Holy Spirit his biblical role in consecration and in the Church’s life.
It locates the Eucharist within the whole liturgy and eschatological vision of the Church rather than a moment of consecration.
Catholic theologians historically argued that without the precision of transubstantiation, the Orthodox view could drift (as with Lucaris); the epiclesis controversy disputed when the change occurs.
Protestants raise the same objections as against transubstantiation: Christ’s body is in heaven and faith, not change of elements, is decisive.
Some argue the 1672 adoption of metousiosis shows the Orthodox could not, in fact, avoid scholastic categories.
positions/orthodox-eucharistic-mystery/r: Orthodox reply that the whole anaphora consecrates, so the institution narrative and epiclesis need not be set against each other.
They argue the Spirit’s descent "makes" the gifts Christ’s body precisely so that believers ascend to the Kingdom, answering the "body in heaven" objection.
positions/orthodox-eucharistic-mystery/c: Shapes Orthodox worship: frequent communion movements, infant communion, leavened bread (azymes controversy with the West).
A largely shared realism makes Catholic–Orthodox Eucharistic disagreement chiefly about authority and communion, not presence.
The 2001 Addai and Mari decision allowed limited eucharistic sharing between Chaldean Catholics and the Assyrian Church of the East.
positions/lutheran-sacramental-union/one: Christ’s true body and blood are truly present "in, with and under" the bread and wine, which remain, and are received orally by all communicants, believers to blessing and unbelievers to judgement.
positions/lutheran-sacramental-union/cor: "This is my body" must be taken literally: the bread is Christ’s body by sacramental union.
The bread and wine are not annihilated or transubstantiated; both realities are present.
All who receive eat and drink Christ’s body and blood with the mouth (manducatio oralis), including the unworthy (manducatio indignorum).
The presence depends on Christ’s word and institution, not on the faith of the recipient or the merit of the minister.
The Supper is a gift and testament for the forgiveness of sins, not a sacrifice offered to God.
positions/lutheran-sacramental-union/key: Small Catechism, Sacrament of the Altar
positions/lutheran-sacramental-union/ori: Developed by Martin Luther in debates with Karlstadt and Zwingli (That These Words of Christ Still Stand Firm, 1527; Confession Concerning Christ’s Supper, 1528), and given confessional form in the Augsburg Confession X (1530), the Wittenberg Concord (1536) and the Formula of Concord VII (1577). Luther defended it partly via the communication of attributes: Christ’s glorified humanity shares the divine power to be present wherever he wills.
positions/lutheran-sacramental-union/str: It is the most straightforward reading of Christ’s words, and Paul’s "guilty of the body and blood" (1 Cor 11:27) implies the unworthy really receive it.
It affirms real presence without dependence on Aristotelian substance theory.
Christ’s promise and power ground assurance: the gift does not depend on our faith or spiritual ascent.
Reformed critics argue that the ubiquity or multipresence of Christ’s body compromises the true humanity of Christ (a body must be in one place) and edges towards Eutychianism.
Catholics argue that "this is my body" cannot also be "this is bread", so sacramental union contradicts the plain sense it claims to defend.
Zwinglians argue the flesh "profiteth nothing" (John 6:63) and that Jesus also said "I am the door" without being wood.
positions/lutheran-sacramental-union/res: Lutherans reply that the communication of attributes (genus maiestaticum) is a proper consequence of the personal union of Christ’s natures (Chalcedon).
They cite Paul’s language "the bread which we break, is it not the communion of the body of Christ?" (1 Cor 10:16), which holds bread and body together.
positions/lutheran-sacramental-union/con: Caused the failure of the Marburg Colloquy and the lasting Lutheran–Reformed split.
Shaped Lutheran liturgy and piety (frequent communion, retention of vestments and altars).
Partly overcome for European Lutheran and Reformed churches by the Leuenberg Agreement (1973) and in the US by the Formula of Agreement (1997), though rejected by confessional Lutherans (e.g. LCMS).
